solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Shipmaster fine after eclipse cheers part of UK, Westward Ho! (7,4)

indicators.note: an across entry reads west to east, so heading westward means travelling right to left, turning NI round
'fine after' the rest puts OK at the very end, behind everything that comes before it

blocks.note: to cap is to outdo or eclipse

explanation.surface: A cry of 'Westward Ho!' as a ship sets out west, borrowing the title of the Devon novel and village.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name into small chunks and the long cheerful surface falls apart; 'fine after' means OK comes last of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the pirate captain of the Jolly Roger in Peter Pan is a shipmaster.

clue.text: Bit mean (7)

blocks.note: a noun: a piece snipped off, from a plant or a newspaper
an adjective: hurtful, as a remark can be

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs or a phrase ('a bit mean'), but one is a noun and the other an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: a snipped-off piece of a plant or newspaper, and wounding in the way an unkind remark is.

clue.text: Introductions for this writer, up first to speak (6)

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read bottom to top, so ME turns over
'first to speak' is the opening letter of the word speak

blocks.note: this writer = ME, the setter, turned upward

explanation.surface: A writer asks to be allowed to speak first when introductions are made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter referring to themself: ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain but literary synonym: a proem is a preface to a book or speech.

clue.text: Banter like silly kid (5-5)

indicators.note: silly letters behave foolishly and will not stay in their given order

explanation.surface: Someone trades jokes like a daft child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a comparison joining the halves, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang: a toddler is at ankle height, so a small kid is jokingly called this.

clue.text: Loud guide from the south causing a stink (4)

indicators.note: in a down entry, starting from the south means reading from the bottom upward

blocks.note: a fin steers a fish, a surfboard or a rocket

explanation.surface: A noisy tour guide from the south of the country makes a stink.
explanation.walkthrough: FFIN is written upward to fill the light.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: a niff is a bad smell.

clue.text: Utterly dominate game, Chelsea full backs ultimately making mistakes (3,5)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take each word's final letter

blocks.note: to own an opponent is slang for thrashing them
last letters of chelseA, fulL, backS

explanation.surface: A football report: Chelsea's full backs keep erring while the team dominates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full backs' is a football position, but here 'full' and 'backs' are just two words giving their last letters. Chelsea is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative use: scoring into your own net is the classic football blunder, and the phrase now means any self-inflicted mistake.

clue.text: Taxing financial gain (7)

blocks.note: an adjective: exhausting, as a steep climb is
a noun: a big profit, as in 'make a ___'

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, 'taxing financial gain' sounds like a tax policy; split it after 'Taxing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally exhausting, and the idiom for a sudden large profit.

clue.text: Having gone into herd, animal doctor misses opening in horse’s joint (7)

indicators.note: the shortened VET has gone into the herd word, so it sits inside FLOCK
the opening of a word is its first letter, which VET misses

blocks.note: a flock is a herd of sheep or goats

explanation.surface: A vet goes into the herd and fails to spot a problem with a horse's leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' is not a gap in a joint but the first letter of VET.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain anatomy: the joint just above a horse's hoof, with its tuft of hair.

clue.text: Female set Down clue, originally camouflaged to describe Liberal hippy (6,5)

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the clue's first letter is used
to describe a circle is to draw round it, so HID goes round L

blocks.note: to lower is to set down

explanation.surface: A woman writes a Down clue, disguising it to describe a liberal hippy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down clue' tempts you to look at the grid; it is really LOWER then C.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym from the 1960s, when hippies wore flowers as symbols of peace.

clue.text: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers occasionally fear the end for Cormoran Strike (3,4)

definitions.text: Maybe loyal group of Rowling readers

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of fear shows up
the end of Cormoran is its last letter

blocks.note: odd letters F, A of fear

explanation.surface: J.K. Rowling's readers fear the fate of her detective Cormoran Strike.
explanation.walkthrough: Cormoran Strike is Rowling's detective (written as Robert Galbraith), so 'Strike' reads as a name; here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'Maybe': devoted readers of one author form an organised following.

clue.text: I put notices up for Spooner, yet quarrel (11)

definitions.note: the definition is the person speaking about their job; the answer is the noun for that person

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version of the phrase swaps them

blocks.note: yet = still; it gives up its ST sound and takes the B
quarrel = bicker; it hands over its B and collects the ST

explanation.surface: A man pins up notices yet still argues.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' is the person being defined, talking about their job.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a posted notice, and the person who pastes them on walls describes their work this way.

clue.text: Arresting European suspect, impound drug smoked here (5,3)

indicators.note: to arrest is to hold, so the jumbled word holds E inside it
suspect letters are dubious, not to be trusted in their given order

explanation.surface: Police arrest a European suspect and seize his drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: E slips between the D and N of the jumbled IMPOUND. 'Suspect' is a noun in the surface and the anagram signal in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the drug is named in the answer's first word, and a den is the place where it is smoked.

clue.text: Gathering agents must infiltrate mostly unescorted? (6)

indicators.note: agents infiltrate by getting inside, so CIA goes inside the other word
mostly means most but not all, so SOLO loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Spies must slip into a party where people have come without partners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathering' looks like a verb (collecting agents), but it is a noun: a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: an informal get-together of a club or group.

clue.text: One seen around bed and seat following one’s husband (6,4)

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references

explanation.surface: Someone sits by the bed next to their husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' suggests a bedroom, but it is the sea bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a fish that lives near the sea bed is one seen around it.

clue.text: Part of cooked breakfast, say, extremely generous (4)

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word, its outermost letters

explanation.surface: A generous serving as part of a fry-up.
explanation.walkthrough: A cooked breakfast is the British fry-up of bacon, sausage, toast and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: fried or scrambled, they are one standard item on the plate.

clue.text: Ignores the wishes of stupid boss, idle git wasting time (10)

indicators.note: stupid letters behave foolishly and will not stay in their given order
wasting means losing, so GIT loses T, the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A lazy boss is ignored by his staff.
explanation.walkthrough: A git is British slang for an unpleasant or foolish person.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to refuse someone the favour or compliance they want.

clue.text: Undone by pressure, a bowler playing poorly (5,3)

indicators.note: something undone has been taken apart, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler cracks under pressure and bowls badly.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the bowler delivers the ball; here the word is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from golf: scoring worse than the standard means performing under your usual form.

clue.text: Here, secured by sailor on bow of clipper, is one of two anchors? (10)

indicators.note: something secured by a sailor is held in their grip, so PRESENT sits inside OS
the bow is the front of a ship, so the first letter of clipper
in an across entry, the rest is placed on C, coming after it

explanation.surface: A sailor on a clipper ship secures one of its two anchors.
explanation.walkthrough: The anchors are not a ship's but a news programme's presenters, which the question mark signals.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun on anchor, the presenter of a broadcast: sharing that role with one other person.

clue.text: Quiet pal so excited about rook in trees (7)

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up out of their order
about means around, so the jumbled letters go round R

explanation.surface: A quiet friend gets excited about a rook nesting in the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: The rook is not the bird in the trees but R from chess.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: tall, fast-growing trees of the willow family.

clue.text: Case online tuition covers (4)

indicators.note: the phrase covers, or contains, the answer inside it

explanation.surface: A legal case about online teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is a crossword favourite, from French, for a small ornamental holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A specific kind of case: a small decorative one for needles, pins or cosmetics.

clue.text: Firm to accommodate working after dark very soon? (7)

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to take them in, so TIGHT takes ON inside

explanation.surface: A firm takes on extra work in the evening to be ready soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as a company; it is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description, marked by '?': the coming evening is both after dark and not far off.

clue.text: Prior to game of chance, lid of Biro is under the table (6)

indicators.note: prior to means before, so B is placed ahead of the game
the lid sits on top, so the first letter in a down entry

blocks.note: lotto, a lottery or bingo-like game

explanation.surface: Before the lottery draw, the cap of a pen has fallen under the table.
explanation.walkthrough: A Biro is a ballpoint pen. 'Under the table' is the drunk's position, not the pen lid's.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone who has drunk so much they slide off their chair is very drunk.

clue.text: Ad-lib technique in rally cut short (6)

indicators.note: a word cut short has had its tail trimmed, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: IMPROVE (to rally, recover) without its E

explanation.surface: A political rally is cut short and speakers have to ad-lib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rally' is a verb: a patient who rallies gets better.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for improvisation: performing unscripted, making it up on the spot.

clue.text: Author Deighton’s visiting Omsk, busy Russian city (8)

indicators.note: a visitor goes into a place, so LENS goes into the other letters
busy letters are bustling about out of their order

explanation.surface: Len Deighton visits two Russian cities, Omsk being lively.
explanation.walkthrough: Omsk is a real Russian city, so it looks like the definition; it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an old city on the Dnieper in western Russia.

clue.text: Sudden shot (4)

blocks.note: an adjective: done on the spur of the moment, as an election can be

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sudden shot' reads as a gunshot; split it into an adjective and a photo.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally, sudden or hurried, and a casual photograph.

clue.text: Poker Face, absolutely rubbish (7)

blocks.note: dead = absolutely, as in dead right
to pan is to rubbish, criticise harshly

explanation.surface: A reviewer calls the song Poker Face absolutely rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to the Lady Gaga song, but the definition is simply an expressionless face.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym phrase: a face that gives nothing away, as a card player's must.

clue.text: Figure Italian team will include Angelo in the middle (7)

indicators.note: to include is to take in, so INTER takes GE inside it
Angelo in the middle is just its central letters

explanation.surface: An Italian football team signs a player called Angelo to play in midfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' could be a shape or a person; here it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain mathematical sense: a whole number is a figure.

clue.text: Ailment cheeky son lies about? That catches relative out for starters (5,6)

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the cheeky son lies facing the other way
to catch is to hold, so THAT holds RO inside it
starters come first, so take the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A cheeky son fakes an illness to skip school, until a relative catches him out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the first half, but the second half is still wordplay: 'That' is not a pointer back but letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sore throat caused by streptococcus bacteria is one ailment.
